questions.subject: GOVERNANCE
questions.microTopic: Appointment to various Constitutional posts; Constitutional Bodies (powers, functions and responsibilities)
questions.microtag: Describe, State, Attorney General of India
questions.questionText: Describe the appointment process, duties, and functions of the Attorney General of India. Also, state  the restrictions governing the functioning of the office.

answers.answerText:
| **Approach:** • Introduce the answer by giving a brief background about the post of Attorney General of India.
• In the body, describe the appointment process, duties and functions of the Attorney General of India.
• Next, state the restricting governing the functioning of the office.
• Conclude the answer by impressing on the fact that despite being a part of the Union Executive, the Attorney General is not a government servant. | | --- | **Article 76** of the Constitution creates the **office of Attorney General for India**, who is the **highest law officer** in the country. **Appointed by the President,** the AGI must be **qualified to become a judge of the Supreme** **Court**. She holds office **during the pleasure of the President.** As a **convention**, AGI **submits her resignation** **to the President** upon the **change of government**. As the **chief law officer of the Government of India,** the Attorney General has been assigned the following **duties and functions**: 1. a) Advise the government** on **legal matters** referred by the **President (**advice on grant of full GST compensation to states). Performs **duties of a legal character** that are assigned to her by the **President.**** 2. a) Appear **on behalf of the Union Government** in all cases in the **Supreme Court** where the Government of India is a party (e.g., ***Anuradha Bhasin case 2020***); b) represent the Union Government in **High Courts,** when required. 3. a) Represents the Government of India in **any reference** made by the **President** to the **Supreme Court** under **Article 143 (**Presidential reference in 2G case); b) discharge the **functions** conferred on her by the **Constitution or any law (**Contempt of Courts Act 1971). 4. a) Participate in parliamentary proceedings** as and when required, without any **voting rights; b) **assist the Court** in the interest of **rightful administration of justice (**Taj Corridor case). However, certain **limitations** have been placed in the office: 1. a) The Attorney General is **disallowed** to advise or argue **cases against the Union Government;** b) she must not **advise or argue** in cases where she is supposed to advise **for the Union Government.** 2. a) She must not **defend accused persons in criminal proceedings** without the **permission of the** **Union Government;** b) to prevent **conflict of interests,** she must not accept **appointment as a** **director in any company** without government permission. 3. a) The Attorney General must refrain from **advising any government body** unless the **proposal** or a reference in this regard is **received through the Ministry of Law and Justice**. Despite being a **member of the Union Executive,** the Attorney General of India **does not fall** under the category of **government servants.** As a result, **neither** is she a **full-time legal counsel** for the Union Government **nor** is she **debarred from private practice.** ***(351 words)*** **Q.****2) Reorganization of States remains a parliamentary prerogative in India, with the Constitution assigning** **only a consultative role to State legislatures. Examine.** ***Approach: Introduce the answer with articles of the Constitution dealing with reorganization of states. In*** ***the body of answer, examine the factors due to which the reorganization of states remains a parliamentary*** ***prerogative in India, with the Constitution assigning only a consultative role to the State legislatures.*** ***Conclude by highlighting the constitutional safeguards in place to protect the interests of the state.*** **Article 2** of the Constitution deals with **admission or establishment of new states** while **Article 3** deals **with** **alteration** of areas, **boundaries or names** of existing states. These provisions establish India as an **indestructible union of destructible states**, a feature of **federal state** with **unitary bias.** While the **Constitution provides substantial power to State Assemblies**, reorganization of states remains a parliamentary prerogative in India. The State legislatures have been assigned only a consultative role in the process due to the following factors: 1. While the **drafting of the Constitution**, India was emerging from colonial **rule.** Given the challenges of a **nascent democracy** and the **recent partition**, constitution-makers favoured **centralized control** over **state reorganization.** They believed it was crucial to prevent **balkanization** and preserve the unity **and integrity** of India. 2. After independence, **existing boundaries** were seen as **arbitrary remnants of colonial rule**. **Redrawing boundaries** was recognized as **necessary** due to this reason. However, involving the states directly risked **prioritizing regional over national interests**. Parliamentary control ensured balanced decision-making for **national cohesion and stability.** E.g., Patiala and East Punjab States Union **(PEPSU) merged into Punjab** state in 1956. 3. **Administrative convenience** and **practicality** were also important considerations. Parliamentary control over the matter ensures a **standardized process** across the country. It provides **consistency** in dealing with **demands for new states or** alterations in state boundaries. Also, **regional aspirations** have been **accommodated by the Parliament** from time to time. E.g., reorganization of NE states, creation of **Telangana (2014)**. Nevertheless, the framers of the Constitution put **safeguards in place** to protect the interest of the **affected** **states**. Any bill for the reorganisation of the states requires **prior recommendation** of the President. The concerned State Assembly has to be **consulted** by the President and the bill must also be **scrutinized and passed** by the **Council of States**.***(297 words)***

questions.subject: POLITY
questions.microTopic: Salient features of the Representation of People's Act
questions.questionText: “Structural weaknesses and implementation challenges continue to undermine the effectiveness of  the Tenth Schedule of the Constitution”. Comment.

answers.answerText:
| **Approach:** • Introduce the answer by giving a brief background of the Tenth Schedule of the Constitution.
• In the body, first highlight its successes.
• Next, point out how structural weaknesses and implementation challenges continue to undermine its effectiveness.
• the ways in which it has failed to achieve its objectives.
• Conclude with suggestions to reform the law. | | --- | **Tenth Schedule of the Constitution**, also known as the **anti-defection law**, was inserted via the **52****nd** **Constitutional Amendment (1985).** It contains provisions to **disqualify legislators** from their membership on **grounds of defection**. It has played an important role in **safeguarding the foundations of democracy** in the following ways: 1. The law has **strengthened democratic stability** by reducing **individual defections**. This has led to stable governments and **fewer premature elections** at both central and state levels. 2. The disqualification provision **bars the defectors** from **ministerial positions**. This has effectively reduced **opportunistic party-switching**(Aaya Ram Gaya Ram) driven by the **'lure of office’.** 3. The legislation has improved **party discipline** and **organizational cohesion** through strong **disincentives** against **arbitrary defections**. 4. Ensured respect for **popular mandate** which is often linked to a candidate’s **party affiliation** or **independent status.** 5. The **constitutional framework** established by the law provides a **clear mechanism (**e.g. grounds and procedure for disqualification) for addressing political defections. Despite these positive outcomes, **structural weaknesses** and **implementation challenges** continue to **undermine the law's effectiveness**, as highlighted in the Law Commission's 170th report: 1. a) **Loopholes** in the law (disqualification ceases to be effective on re-election) have been **exploited** to **manufacture mass resignations** (Karnataka) and **destabilize governments** (Madhya Pradesh, Uttarakhand); b) defections have been engineered to **deplete the ranks** of Opposition in the legislature (West Bengal). 2. **Practical challenges** have arisen because of the **Speaker's role** as the **adjudicating authority**. Courts have raised question marks on the **neutrality of the Speaker** (*Keisham Meghchandra Singh* *case 2020*) and **delays in deciding** disqualification petitions (*Maharashtra Speaker case 2020*). 3. a) **Exemption** granted to **merger** of 2/3rd members has been maneuvered to **serve political interests** (Goa); b) The law does not cover **activities outside** the legislature which are contrary to the **spirit of** **the law** (Jignesh Mevani case 2022). 4. a) Party leadership** has been **disproportionately strengthened** through the power to issue **whips**. This has come at the cost of **autonomy** of individual legislators (restricted freedom of speech and conscience) and **intra-party democracy** (can be used to curb dissent);** b) **ambiguous phrases** (“voluntarily gives up membership”) have resulted in **inconsistent interpretation** and **application**. The recommendations of the Halim Committee, NCRWC, and Supreme Court judgments calling for **independent tribunals** and **fixed timelines for decisions** provide a **roadmap for reform**. These **institutional** **changes**, coupled with strengthening **intra-party democracy**, would help realize the **law's original objectives**. (***388 words***) **Q.4)** **While tribunals have their salience in the Indian justice system, they are beset with multiple** **challenges. Elaborate**. ***Approach: Introduce by writing about tribunals and relevant Articles of Constitution. In the body, first*** ***discuss their salience in the Indian justice system. In the next part, mention the multiple challenges they*** ***are beset with. Conclude by highlighting recent developments in the direction of improving their*** ***effectiveness.*** Tribunals are **quasi-judicial bodies** established to adjudicate specific **administrative matters** outlined in **Article 323A**, or **other designated areas (**e.g. taxation, industrial disputes) as specified in **Article 323B.** Tribunals have great **salience** in the Indian justice system, as discussed below: 1. a) Facilitate **speedier disposal** of cases (informal procedures- e.g. guided by principles of natural justice), thereby helping reduce **judicial backlog** (e.g. CAT); b) non-adversarial nature of proceedings** enables more consensual disposal of complicated cases (e.g. NCLT).** 2. a) Bring **domain knowledge** through integration of domain experts, thereby enabling **specialized** **adjudication** (e.g. ITAT); b) provide avenues for **low-cost litigation,** especially to the weaker sections of the society (e.g. Maintenance Tribunals under the Maintenance and Welfare of Parents and Senior Citizens Act, 2007). 3. a) Enhance **access to justice** in far-fetched corners of the country (e.g. through regional benches); b) pioneer **progressive jurisprudence** in emerging areas (e.g. environmental justice- NGT) However, tribunals’ functioning is **beset with multiple challenges:** 1. a) **Executive interference** in functioning (e.g. in appointment of chairpersons/members) violates the principle of **separation of powers;** b) **structural issues** with the tribunals (vacancies, inadequate support staff, infrastructural gaps) reduce their functionality. 2. a) Diversity in **composition, structure and statutes** has created confusion about their powers, jurisdiction and functions, leading to **tribunalization of justice;** b) frequent appeals** against their decisions end up **prolonging** the judicial process, increasing **financial burden** on the parties and causing **judicial delays.**** **Tribunal Reform Act 2021** rationalized the **number of tribunals** to address some of these concerns. However, to ensure these bodies **fulfill their intended mandate**, these reforms must be complemented with the suggestions of the Supreme Court (**judicial impact assessment, National Tribunals Commission)**. ***(302*** ***Words)***

questions.microtag: Discuss, Supreme Court, Environmental issues, Case laws
questions.questionText: “The Supreme Court’s recognition of environmental issues within the constitutional framework has  been a landmark transformation in contemporary Indian legal discourse.” Discuss the statement with the  help of relevant case laws.

answers.answerText:
| **Approach:** • Introduce the answer by giving a brief background of the recent Supreme Court judgement on adverse effects of climate change.
• In the body, discuss the role played by the Indian judiciary in constitutionalization of environmental issues, citing relevant case laws.
• Conclude by highlighting the importance of this constitutionalization. | | --- | In a landmark judgment in **M.K. Ranjitsinh vs. Union of India** (April 2024), the Supreme Court recognized the **'right against adverse effects of climate change'** as a **distinct fundamental right** under **Articles 14 and 21** of the Constitution. This judgment represents a **continuation** of decades of judicial interpretation that has **progressively 'constitutionalized'** environmental protection through various **landmark decisions**, as detailed below: 1. **Constitutional interpretation** expanding **Article 21** to include environmental rights: 1.1. a) The Supreme Court in **M.C. Mehta** v. Union of India (1987) established that the right to life includes the **right to a healthy environment.** It also introduced the **doctrine of absolute** **liability**; b) **Subhash Kumar** v. State of Bihar (1991)** recognized that the right to **pollution-** **free water and air** comes within the purview of Article 21.** 1.2. **Virender Gaur** v. State of Haryana (1995) emphasized that **hygienic environment** is an **integral facet** of right to healthy life, while stressing upon State’s fundamental duty to maintain **ecological balance.** 2. **Public trust doctrine** incorporation through judicial pronouncements: 2.1. a) The landmark case of **M.C. Mehta** v. Kamal Nath (1997) established that **natural resources** are **held in trust** by the government for public use; b) **M.I. Builders** v. Radhey Shyam Sahu (1999) applied this doctrine to protect **public parks**; c) **Intellectuals Forum** v. State of AP (2006) extended the doctrine to protect **water bodies** from **encroachment.** 3. **“Precautionary Principle”** and “**Polluter Pays Principle”** integration: 3.1. a) **Vellore Citizens Welfare Forum** v. Union of India (1996) declared these principles as part of **environmental law**; b) **Indian Council for Enviro-Legal Action** v. Union of India (1996) applied the polluter pays principle to make **industries liable** for **environmental restoration.** 3.2. **A.P. Pollution Control Board** v. Prof. M.V. Nayudu (1999) established that lack of **scientific** **certainty** cannot justify postponing environmental **protection measures**, placing the **burden** **of proof** on parties proposing potentially **harmful activities** (framework for applying precautionary principle). 4. **Procedural innovations** enhancing environmental justice: 4.1. Expansion of **Public Interest Litigation (PIL)** in environmental matters through cases like **Rural Litigation and Entitlement Kendra** v. State of UP (1985)** enabling citizens to approach courts for environmental protection.** 4.2. a) Adoption of **continuing mandamus** in T.N. Godavarman v Union of India, allowing courts to **monitor environmental compliance**; b) establishment of **specialized benches** and **National Green Tribunal** through **judicial recommendations** and consequent legislation. (e.g., National Green Tribunal Act, 2010) 5. **Sustainable Development** framework development: 5.1. **T.N. Godavarman Thirumulpad** v. Union of India series established a comprehensive **forest** **conservation framework** (e.g., expanded the definition of **'forest' beyond statutory** **boundaries**) 5.2. a) **Narmada Bachao Andolan** v. Union of India (2000) balanced **development needs** with **environmental protection** (explaining the concept of sustainable development); b) **M.C.** **Mehta** v. Union of India (2004) (Delhi CNG case) promoted **sustainable urban transport** systems. This **evolution** of environmental jurisprudence has **operationalized the mandate** of Article 48A, transforming the **Directive Principle** of environmental protection into **concrete mechanisms** for **environmental** **stewardship** and **ecological preservation.** ***(454 words)***

questions.questionText: Explain the structure of the Parliamentary Committee system. How far have the Departmentally  Related Standing Committees (DRSCs) helped in the institutionalisation of Indian Parliament?

answers.answerText:
| **Approach:** • Introduce the answer with a brief background of the Parliamentary Committee system.
• In the body, first explain the structure of the same.
• Next, highlight the extent to which they have helped in the institutionalization of Indian Parliament.
• Conclude by suggesting reforms to improve their functioning. | | --- | Parliamentary Committee is a group of MPs who are **appointed or elected** by the House or **nominated by the** **chairperson of the house.** It studies and deliberates on **a range of subject matters**, Bills, and budgets of the ministries. It works under **the chairperson’s** **direction** and presents its **report to the chairperson or the** **House.** By their nature, Parliamentary Committees are of the following **two kinds**: 1. **Standing Committees**: a) **Permanent and regular committees,** which are **re-constituted from** **time to time;** b) three types of committees come under this category - **Financial Committees (**Public Accounts Committee**), Departmentally related Standing Committees (**Committee on Commerce) and **Other Parliamentary Standing Committees (**Business Advisory Committee). 2. **Ad hoc Committees:** a) Appointed for a **specific purpose** and **cease to exist** when the task is **finished;** b) divided into two categories- **Inquiry Committees (**JPC on 2G spectrum case) and **Advisory Committees (**JPC on Waqf Bill). **Departmentally Related Standing Committees** (DRSCs) cover under their **jurisdiction** all the **Ministries/** **Departments of the Government of India** and comprise **members** from both the **Lok Sabha (21)** and the **Rajya** **Sabha (10).** They have played a crucial role in the **institutionalization of Parliament** in the following ways: 1. a) Consider the **demand for grants** of various ministries, thus aiding **effective debate over the** **Budget**; b) **examine** in-depth the **bills** referred to them, analyze **policies** and provide their **suggestions to strengthen** the same. 2. a) Provisions of **anti-defection laws** are **not applicable** to Committee proceedings. This allows individual **MPs to freely voice their opinions**; b) **closed-door nature of proceedings** enables members to **diverge from party line** and r**each consensus** on critical matters. 3. a) Provide a platform for **domain experts** to consult with public representatives and provide their inputs in policy making; b) reflect the principles of **direct democracy** by engaging with **grassroots** **organizations, civil society groups** and the **general public**. 4. a) Help make up for the l**oss of time** (disruptions, adjournments) on the **floor of the House**; b) **continuous nature of the functioning** of Committees compensates for the **steady decline in the** **sittings of the Parliament** (average annual sitting of the 17th Lok Sabha-55 days). 5. a) Enable the **Rajya Sabha** in exercising **financial control** over the Executive indirectly; b) facilitate **intellectual development of individual MPs** who can focus on particular policy domains and build expertise therein; c) make space for **opposition** to contribute to **government functioning**. However, the following **factors** have impeded the ability of the DRSCs in this regard: 1. a) **Decrease** in the number of bills being referred to the Committees (only 16% in the 17th Lok Sabha); b) **non-binding** nature of the **recommendations** of the Committee. 2. a) Decline** in the working of the Committees (delays in submitting reports, lesser number of sittings for specific bills, lower attendance of members);** b) growing instances of **divisions along partisan lines** in Committee proceedings (Data Protection Bill, Waqf Bill). 3. a) Handicaps in functioning due to **absence** of **standing research support** (highlighted by NCRWC); b) non-consideration of **members’ own expertise** while nominating them to different committees. This, coupled with **short tenure** (1 year), leads to **ad-hocism** in their functioning. The DRSC System is a path-breaking endeavour of **parliamentary surveillance over administration**. There is a need to improve the functioning of these **“mini-Parliaments”** through sustained **secretarial and research** **support**. This will allow them to better **guide the Executive** in the achievement of **long-term national goals**. (***404 words***)

questions.microtag: Critically discuss, Codification, Parliamentary privileges, India
questions.questionText: Critically discuss the need for the codification of parliamentary privileges in the country.

answers.answerText:
| **Approach:** • Introduce the answer by highlighting the different sources of parliamentary privileges and the absence of a definitive Code for the same.
• In the body, discuss the need for the codification of parliamentary privileges in the country, highlighting both the positives and negatives of the same.
• Conclude by underlining the need to incorporate international best practices in the exercise of privileges. | | --- | **Article 105 (3)** empowers **Parliament to define the Parliamentary Privileges**. However, in the **absence of** **such a law**, parliamentary privileges continue to be derived from diverse **sources**-**Constitution, statutes,** **judicial interpretation, rules of procedure** and established **conventions**. Several experts have flagged the **ambiguity** and **the potential for their misuse** in the absence of a definitive Code of Parliamentary privileges. They have argued in **favour of such a code on account** of the following reasons: 1. The present system **equates Indian Parliament** and **British House of Commons** (despite the reference to Section 15 of 44th Amendment). While the latter is regarded as **sovereign**, the former is subject to **constitutional limitations**. A Code of Parliamentary Privileges will **uphold the supremacy** **of the Constitution** as opposed to the supremacy of Parliament. 2. a) Codification can **remove the uncertainty in their application**. This uncertainty creates **potential** **for misuse** by curbing the **freedom of speech** of the citizens (Karnataka Assembly case 2017); b) It can strengthen the **right of information** of the citizens (definitive guidelines to prevent arbitrary redaction of parliamentary proceedings); c) such a system will uphold the ideals of **constitutionalism** (limited power). 3. a) A codified framework can also provide **safeguards against attempts to stifle dissent** or suppress **minority voices** within the legislature. Protecting the **rights of individual parliamentarians** can strengthen the democratic principles of representation and pluralism; b) Clear guidelines and mechanisms would demonstrate the **commitment of the legislature to transparency and fairness**. 4. a) It will delineate the limits and conditions under which privileges can be invoked. This can help prevent the use of privileges as a **shield** to protect MPs from **legitimate scrutiny.** b) such codification will allow the **judiciary to examine the validity of privilege claims** and preserve the constitutional principle of **checks and balances**. Despite the aforementioned advantages of codification, lawmakers have put forward the following **reasons in** **opposition to codification:** 1. a) Codification of privileges is likely to have adverse consequences for the **independence of the** **Parliament** and **separation of powers**; b) any law enacted for codification will be **subject to judicial** **scrutiny** for inconsistency with the **Fundamental Rights** (Patna Searchlight Case). 2. a) Any legislation aimed at codification will be a reflection of the **will of the current Executive** which holds majority. Such a law may curtail the **privileges of Opposition members**; b) crystallization of privileges in a code may **reduce the interpretive power of the Presiding officers.** This will impact their ability to respond to **practical challenges in the functioning** of the House. Several **other democratic countries such as Australia** have taken concrete steps in the direction of **codification of Parliamentary privileges.** Until such time as codification takes place, **India can incorporate** **best practices** from other countries. This will help ensure that **safeguarding Parliamentary privileges** does not conflict with **rights of citizens and accountability of members**. (***453 words***)
